title: Philosophy of Mathematics: Are Numbers Real?
subtitle: Discovered or invented, and why does it work so well on the world?
objectives: By the end you will be able to state Benacerraf's dilemma and explain why it makes the question 'are numbers real?' so hard
By the end you will be able to compare Platonism, formalism and intuitionism, including the impact of Gödel's incompleteness theorems
By the end you will be able to work through a non-constructive proof and explain why an intuitionist rejects it
By the end you will be able to reconstruct the Quine-Putnam indispensability argument, the enhanced version using periodical cicadas, and Field's fictionalist reply
By the end you will be able to assess explanations of the 'unreasonable effectiveness' of mathematics in physics
hook:
In 1928 the British physicist Paul Dirac wrote down an equation to describe the electron that was consistent with both quantum mechanics and Einstein's special relativity. The mathematics had an awkward feature: it allowed solutions that seemed to describe electrons with negative energy. Dirac eventually took them seriously, proposing a new particle with the electron's mass but opposite charge. In 1932 Carl Anderson found exactly such a particle, the positron, in cosmic ray tracks. Mathematics written on paper had predicted a piece of the universe no one had seen.

How is that possible? The physicist Eugene Wigner, in a famous 1960 essay, called it 'the unreasonable effectiveness of mathematics in the natural sciences'. Numbers, functions and equations do not seem to be anywhere: you cannot trip over the number 7 or weigh the square root of minus one. Yet they describe the world with astonishing accuracy. On Day 3 you met Pythagoras, who thought that all things are number. On Day 11 Plato placed mathematical objects in a realm of eternal Forms. On Day 69 Frege and Russell tried to reduce mathematics to logic. This lesson asks the question directly: are numbers real? And if they are, how could we possibly know anything about them?

sections.heading: Benacerraf's Dilemma
sections.body:
The modern debate was framed by the American philosopher **Paul Benacerraf** in a 1973 paper, 'Mathematical Truth'. He argued that any account of mathematics must meet two demands that seem to pull in opposite directions.

The first is **semantic**. We should interpret mathematical sentences the same way we interpret other sentences. 'There is a city larger than London' is true because there exists such a city. By parity, 'there is a prime number larger than 100' should be true because there exists such a number. So mathematical truth seems to require that mathematical objects exist. And they are strange objects: **abstract**, meaning not located in space or time and not causally active.

The second is **epistemic**. Our account of mathematical *knowledge* should be continuous with our account of other knowledge. Usually, we know about things because they causally affect us: light bounces off the tree and into our eyes. But abstract objects, by definition, affect nothing. So how could we ever come to know about them? Benacerraf assumed a causal theory of knowledge, now less popular, but Hartry Field restated the challenge without it: explain why our mathematical beliefs *reliably* match facts that are causally isolated from us.

The dilemma is this. Theories that give mathematics a straightforward semantics (there really are numbers) make mathematical knowledge mysterious. Theories that make mathematical knowledge easy to explain (mathematics is just rules we invented, or mental constructions) seem to give a strange semantics, on which 'there is a prime larger than 100' doesn't mean what it appears to mean. Every position below grasps one horn or tries to slip between them.

sections.heading: Platonism: Mathematics Is Discovered
sections.body:
**Mathematical Platonism** grasps the first horn. Numbers, sets and functions really exist, as abstract objects independent of human minds and language. Mathematicians *discover* truths about them, rather as astronomers discover truths about distant galaxies. The theorem that there are infinitely many primes (proved by Euclid around 300 BCE) was true before anyone proved it and would be true if humans had never existed.

**Gottlob Frege** (Day 69) held that numbers are objects, and that arithmetic is objective in the way that the North Sea is objective, not in the way that an idea in someone's head is. The logician **Kurt Gödel** (1906–1978) went further. In a 1964 supplement to his paper 'What Is Cantor's Continuum Problem?' he wrote that despite their remoteness from sense experience, we do have something like a perception of the objects of set theory, as seen from the fact that the axioms force themselves upon us as being true. Many mathematicians report this feeling: mathematics resists and surprises them. The number theorist G. H. Hardy (*A Mathematician's Apology*, 1940) agreed that mathematical reality lies outside us.

Platonism explains three things well: the **objectivity** of mathematics (mathematicians across cultures reach the same results), its apparent **necessity** (2 + 2 could not have been 5), and its straightforward **semantics**.

Its great weakness is the epistemic horn of Benacerraf's dilemma. If numbers are outside space and time, what is Gödel's 'something like a perception'? Critics see appeals to intuition as a label for the mystery, not an explanation.

Benacerraf also posed a second puzzle in 'What Numbers Could Not Be' (1965). Modern mathematics can define the natural numbers as sets in several equally good ways. On one (Zermelo's), 2 is the set containing the set containing the empty set. On another (von Neumann's), 2 is the set containing the empty set and the set containing the empty set. Which is the number 2 *really*? There seems to be no fact of the matter. So, Benacerraf concluded, numbers cannot be particular objects at all. What matters is only the **structure**: the pattern of positions in a sequence. This idea, **mathematical structuralism**, developed by Stewart Shapiro and Michael Resnik, holds that mathematics studies structures, and a number is just a position in one. (Compare structural realism in science, from lesson 3.)

sections.heading: Formalism and Gödel's Theorems
sections.body:
**Formalism** grasps the epistemic horn. In its crudest form, **game formalism**, mathematics is the manipulation of symbols according to rules, like chess. Asking whether the number 3 'exists' is like asking whether the bishop exists outside the game. Mathematical knowledge is just knowledge of what follows from what under the rules, which is no more mysterious than knowing how a knight moves. Frege objected that chess says nothing about the world, whereas arithmetic counts apples and builds bridges; a meaningless game would not be so useful.

A much more sophisticated formalism was the programme of the German mathematician **David Hilbert** (1862–1943). Around 1900, paradoxes such as Russell's (Day 69) suggested that Cantor's revolutionary theory of infinite sets might be inconsistent. He declared in 1925 that no one shall expel us from the paradise that Cantor has created. His plan was to formalise all of mathematics as an axiomatic system of symbols, and then prove, using only simple, uncontroversial **finitary** reasoning about finite strings of symbols, that this system could never produce a contradiction.

In 1931 **Kurt Gödel** proved his **incompleteness theorems**, which showed that Hilbert's programme, in its original form, could not succeed.

- **First incompleteness theorem**: any consistent formal system strong enough to express basic arithmetic contains statements that can be neither proved nor disproved within it. Gödel constructed such a sentence which, informally, says of itself 'I am not provable in this system'. If the system is consistent, the sentence is not provable, and so (on the standard interpretation) it is true.
- **Second incompleteness theorem**: such a system cannot prove its own consistency.

So truth in arithmetic outruns provability in any single formal system, and mathematics cannot certify its own consistency from within. Gödel himself took this as support for Platonism: there are arithmetic truths that no formal game captures, so arithmetic must be about something beyond the rules. Formalists reply that the theorems show only that no single system is complete, not that numbers exist.

sections.heading: Intuitionism, with a Worked Example
sections.body:
A third view, **intuitionism**, was founded by the Dutch mathematician **L. E. J. Brouwer** (1881–1966). Brouwer held that mathematics is a free creation of the human mind, built up by mental **construction** in time, starting from the intuition of one moment following another. A mathematical object exists only if we can construct it; a statement is true only if we have a proof of it. (Kant, Day 55, had similarly grounded arithmetic in the intuition of time.)

This has a dramatic consequence. Classical logic accepts the **law of excluded middle**: for any statement P, either P or not-P is true. Brouwer rejected it for infinite domains. If we have neither a proof of P nor a proof of not-P, we have no right to assert 'P or not-P'.

Here is a famous classical proof that shows what is at stake. **Claim**: there exist irrational numbers *a* and *b* such that *a* raised to the power *b* is rational.

**Proof**: Consider the number √2 raised to the power √2. Either it is rational or it is irrational (excluded middle).

1. If it is rational, take *a* = √2 and *b* = √2. Both are irrational, and *a* to the power *b* is rational. Done.
2. If it is irrational, take *a* = √2 to the power √2, and *b* = √2. Then *a* to the power *b* = √2 to the power (√2 × √2) = √2 squared = 2, which is rational. Done.

Either way, such numbers exist. The proof is classically valid and elegant, but it does not tell us *which* pair works. To an intuitionist, this is not a proof of existence at all. It proves that a certain disjunction leads to the conclusion, without constructing the object. (The Gelfond-Schneider theorem of 1934 later showed case 2 is the true one, but that took far deeper mathematics.)

Most mathematicians did not follow Brouwer. Hilbert complained in 1927 that taking the law of excluded middle from the mathematician would be like forbidding the astronomer the telescope or the boxer the use of his fists. But constructive mathematics has had a remarkable afterlife in computer science: a constructive proof that something exists can be turned into an algorithm that finds it, and modern proof assistants are often built on constructive logics.

sections.heading: The Indispensability Argument and the Cicadas
sections.body:
A different route to Platonism comes from science. The **Quine-Putnam indispensability argument**, developed by **W. V. O. Quine** and **Hilary Putnam** in the 1960s and 1970s, runs:

1. We ought to believe in the existence of all and only the entities that are indispensable to our best scientific theories.
2. Mathematical entities (numbers, functions, sets) are indispensable to our best scientific theories.
3. Therefore, we ought to believe in mathematical entities.

Premise 1 draws on Quine's **confirmational holism** (the web of belief, Day 74): theories face evidence as a whole, so the mathematics woven into physics is confirmed along with it.

In 2005 Alan Baker gave an **enhanced indispensability argument**: mathematics does not only describe the world; it sometimes **explains** it. His example is the periodical cicadas of North America, whose life cycles last 13 or 17 years, both prime numbers. Biologists have proposed that prime cycles help the cicadas avoid predators or competitors with shorter periodic cycles.

Let us see why. Two cycles coincide every **least common multiple** of their lengths. Suppose predators have cycles of 2 to 6 years.

- A 12-year cicada meets the 2-, 3-, 4- and 6-year predators every 12 years (and the 5-year predator every 60).
- A 13-year cicada meets the 2-year predator only every 26 years, the 3-year every 39, the 4-year every 52, the 5-year every 65 and the 6-year every 78.

Because a prime has no factors other than 1 and itself, its least common multiple with any smaller number is as large as possible. The explanation of why cicadas have prime periods seems to depend on a fact about numbers. If we believe in what does the explaining in our best explanations, says Baker, we should believe in numbers.

The most ambitious reply came from **Hartry Field** in *Science Without Numbers* (1980). Field argued that mathematics is **not** indispensable. He showed how to restate Newtonian gravitational theory without reference to numbers, using only relations among points of space-time. Mathematics, he concluded, is useful because it is **conservative**: adding it to a scientific theory never lets you derive new claims about the physical world that you couldn't derive without it; it is a powerful shortcut. On Field's **fictionalism**, sentences like '2 + 2 = 4' are literally false (since there are no numbers), but true *in the story of mathematics*, as 'Sherlock Holmes lived on Baker Street' is true in the stories. Critics doubt the programme extends to quantum mechanics.

**Penelope Maddy** attacked premise 1: scientists do not treat every posit of a successful theory as confirmed. Atoms were indispensable to nineteenth-century chemistry, yet many doubted them until Perrin's experiments (lesson 3).

sections.heading: The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Mathematics
sections.body:
Return to Dirac and the positron. Wigner's 1960 essay pointed to cases where mathematics developed for purely internal reasons turned out to describe physical reality. Complex numbers, invented to solve equations and long regarded as 'imaginary', are now built into the foundations of quantum mechanics. The non-Euclidean geometries of the nineteenth century, explored as pure logical possibilities, became the language of Einstein's general relativity. G. H. Hardy boasted in 1940 that number theory had no military or practical use; since the 1970s it has underpinned public-key cryptography, which secures internet banking and, yes, military communications.

Why should this happen? Several answers are on offer, each tied to a position in this lesson.

- **Platonist / Pythagorean**: the physical world has a mathematical structure because it instantiates, or even is, a mathematical structure. The physicist Max Tegmark's **mathematical universe hypothesis** (*Our Mathematical Universe*, 2014) claims that physical reality literally is a mathematical object. This is Pythagoras updated (Day 3); it struggles to say what makes one structure physically real and another not.
- **Selection and origin**: much mathematics was developed from physical problems in the first place (calculus from motion, geometry from land measurement), so its usefulness is less surprising. The computer scientist Richard Hamming, in a 1980 reply to Wigner, added that we see what we look for, choose the mathematics that fits, and forget the vast amounts that do not.
- **Structuralist**: mathematics is the general science of structure and pattern. Any world with regularities will be describable mathematically, because mathematics studies every possible regularity.

None of these fully dissolves the surprise. Selection does not explain why structures explored for their beauty, like complex numbers, later proved essential. Wigner's own conclusion was modest: the fit is a gift we neither understand nor deserve.

keyQuote.text: The miracle of the appropriateness of the language of mathematics for the formulation of the laws of physics is a wonderful gift which we neither understand nor deserve.
keyQuote.source: Eugene Wigner, 'The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Mathematics in the Natural Sciences' (1960)

modernConnection.title: Computer Proofs, Proof Assistants and AI Mathematicians
modernConnection.body:
In 1976 Kenneth Appel and Wolfgang Haken proved the **four colour theorem** (any map can be coloured with four colours so that no neighbouring regions share a colour) with the help of a computer that checked well over a thousand configurations, too many for any human to verify by hand. The philosopher Thomas Tymoczko argued in 1979 that this changed the concept of proof: mathematical knowledge now rested partly on the reliability of machines, an empirical matter, rather than purely on surveyable reasoning.

Today that change has gone much further. **Proof assistants** such as Lean, Coq and Isabelle let mathematicians write proofs in a formal language that a computer checks line by line. Thomas Hales's proof of the Kepler conjecture about sphere packing was formally verified in 2014 in the Flyspeck project. In 2020 the Fields medallist Peter Scholze challenged the community to verify a difficult result of his in Lean, and a team led by Johan Commelin completed the core of the project in 2021, a milestone known as the Liquid Tensor Experiment. AI systems have also begun to produce proofs: in 2024 DeepMind reported that its AlphaProof and AlphaGeometry systems solved problems at the level of a silver medallist at the International Mathematical Olympiad.

The philosophical positions of this lesson look different in this light. Hilbert's dream of mathematics as formal symbol manipulation is literally realised in proof assistants, yet Gödel's theorems still apply to them: no single formal system will capture every truth. Brouwer's constructivism lives on in the logics many proof assistants use, where proofs are programs. And the Platonist question returns: when a machine proves a theorem, has it *discovered* something, or merely derived a string of symbols?

The comparison has limits. Proof assistants check proofs; they do not, by themselves, explain why a result is true or which results are worth seeking. Many mathematicians insist that understanding, not mere verification, is the goal, a view any of our positions can accept.

vocabulary.definition: An object not located in space or time and lacking causal powers, such as a number or a set (if such objects exist).
vocabulary.example: The number 7 is, for a Platonist, an abstract object you cannot see, touch or weigh.

vocabulary.definition: The challenge that a straightforward semantics for mathematics requires abstract objects, while a plausible epistemology seems to rule out knowing about them.
vocabulary.example: Benacerraf's dilemma asks how we can know about numbers if they have no causal effect on us.

vocabulary.definition: The view that mathematical objects exist independently of minds and language, and mathematical truths are discovered.
vocabulary.example: Gödel's mathematical Platonism held that we have something like a perception of sets.

vocabulary.definition: The view that mathematics is fundamentally the manipulation of symbols according to rules, without commitment to abstract objects.
vocabulary.example: Hilbert's formalism aimed to prove mathematics consistent using only finitary reasoning about symbols.

vocabulary.definition: Gödel's 1931 results: consistent formal systems capable of basic arithmetic contain undecidable sentences and cannot prove their own consistency.
vocabulary.example: The incompleteness theorems showed that Hilbert's programme could not succeed in its original form.

vocabulary.definition: Brouwer's view that mathematics is mental construction, so existence requires a construction and the law of excluded middle fails for infinite domains.
vocabulary.example: An intuitionist rejects the √2-to-the-√2 proof because it doesn't say which pair of numbers works.

vocabulary.definition: The Quine-Putnam argument that we should believe in mathematical entities because they are indispensable to our best scientific theories.
vocabulary.example: The cicada example strengthens the indispensability argument by giving mathematics an explanatory role.

vocabulary.definition: Field's view that mathematical statements are literally false, since there are no mathematical objects, but true within the 'story' of mathematics.
vocabulary.example: On fictionalism, '2 + 2 = 4' is like 'Holmes lives on Baker Street': true in the story, not in reality.

thinkingExercise.title: Discovered or Invented?
thinkingExercise.prompt: Test your intuitions about mathematics against the positions in this lesson.
steps: Write down your gut answer: were the infinitely many primes discovered or invented? Then write the best argument for the opposite answer.

Work through the √2-to-the-√2 proof yourself. Do you find it a satisfying proof that such numbers exist? What does your answer suggest about whether you are, at heart, a classical mathematician or an intuitionist?

Redo the cicada calculation for a 15-year cycle against predators of 3 and 5 years. How does the result compare with 13 and 17? Does the explanation really depend on numbers, or on something physical that numbers merely describe?
Choose the answer to Wigner's puzzle you find most convincing and explain in a paragraph why the others fail.

summary: Benacerraf's dilemma: a straightforward semantics needs abstract mathematical objects, but causal isolation makes knowledge of them mysterious.
Platonists (Frege, Gödel, Hardy) explain objectivity and necessity but struggle with knowledge; Benacerraf's multiple set-theoretic numbers motivate structuralism.
Formalism treats mathematics as rule-governed symbol manipulation; Gödel's incompleteness theorems defeated Hilbert's original programme.
Intuitionism treats mathematics as mental construction and rejects excluded middle for infinite domains, refusing non-constructive proofs like the √2-to-the-√2 argument.
The Quine-Putnam indispensability argument and Baker's cicadas support belief in numbers; Field's fictionalism and Maddy's objection resist it.
Wigner's 'unreasonable effectiveness' has Platonist, selectionist and structuralist explanations, none fully dissolving the puzzle.

quiz.question: What are the two demands that generate Benacerraf's dilemma?
options: A uniform semantics for mathematical sentences and a plausible account of mathematical knowledge
quiz.explanation: A literal semantics requires abstract objects; a causal-style epistemology makes knowing them hard.

quiz.question: Benacerraf's 'What Numbers Could Not Be' argued that because numbers can be defined as sets in several equally good ways:
options: Numbers are not particular objects; what matters is their structure
quiz.explanation: With no fact about which set is 2, Benacerraf concluded numbers are positions in a structure, motivating structuralism.

quiz.question: Gödel's first incompleteness theorem shows that any consistent formal system capable of basic arithmetic contains statements it can neither prove nor disprove.
quiz.explanation: This is the first theorem; the second adds that such a system cannot prove its own consistency.

quiz.question: What did Hilbert's programme aim to achieve?
options: A finitary proof that formalised mathematics is consistent
A proof that numbers are physical
A demonstration that excluded middle is false
quiz.explanation: Hilbert wanted to secure Cantor's 'paradise' with a finitary consistency proof; Gödel's second theorem blocked this.

quiz.question: Why does an intuitionist reject the classical proof that irrational a and b exist with a to the power b rational?
options: Because the proof uses a computer
Because it relies on excluded middle and never constructs a specific pair
Because exponents are not allowed in intuitionism
quiz.explanation: The proof shows one of two cases works without saying which, so no object is constructed.

quiz.question: According to Field's fictionalism, '2 + 2 = 4' is literally true because numbers exist in a Platonic realm.
quiz.explanation: Field holds it is literally false (there are no numbers) but true within the story of mathematics.

quiz.question: A 13-year cicada and a 4-year predator coincide every:
quiz.explanation: Since 13 is prime, the least common multiple of 13 and 4 is 52.

quiz.question: Penelope Maddy's objection to the indispensability argument appeals to the fact that:
options: Mathematics is never used in science
Scientists historically doubted posits like atoms even when they were indispensable to theories
Cicadas don't have prime life cycles
quiz.explanation: Maddy argues scientific practice doesn't follow Quine's holism, undermining premise 1.

quiz.question: Which response to Wigner's puzzle says much mathematics arose from physical problems and we tend to notice only the mathematics that fits?
options: The selection and origin response (e.g. Hamming)
quiz.explanation: Hamming and others argue the fit is less surprising given where mathematics came from and how we select it.

quiz.question: Constructive proofs have practical value in computer science because a constructive existence proof can be turned into an algorithm that finds the object.
quiz.explanation: This link between proofs and programs is why constructive logics underlie many proof assistants.

goDeeper.body:
Several further positions and debates repay study. **Neo-Fregeanism** (or neo-logicism), developed by Crispin Wright and Bob Hale, revives Frege's project using **Hume's principle**: the number of Fs equals the number of Gs if and only if the Fs and Gs can be paired off one-to-one. From this principle and second-order logic, all of arithmetic can be derived (a result known as **Frege's theorem**). Neo-Fregeans argue Hume's principle is something like a definition of 'number', so knowing it requires no mysterious perception of abstract objects. Critics, including the 'bad company' objection, point out that principles of the same form can be inconsistent, so we need a criterion for telling good abstraction principles from bad.

In the philosophy of set theory, a lively debate concerns whether questions like Cantor's **continuum hypothesis** (is there a size of infinity between that of the natural numbers and that of the real numbers?) have determinate answers. Gödel and Paul Cohen together showed it can be neither proved nor disproved from the standard axioms (ZFC). Platonists like Hugh Woodin search for new axioms that would settle it. Joel David Hamkins defends a **multiverse** view: there are many equally legitimate set-theoretic universes, in some of which the hypothesis holds and in others not.

Mathematical practice has also become a topic in its own right. Imre Lakatos's *Proofs and Refutations* (1976), a dialogue about Euler's formula for polyhedra, showed that mathematical concepts evolve through counterexamples and revisions, much like scientific theories, a Popperian (Day 72) picture of mathematics. More recently, philosophers have studied **mathematical explanation** within mathematics: why do some proofs explain why a theorem is true, while others merely show that it is?

questions: If a computer proves a theorem no human can survey, do we know the theorem? What kind of knowledge is it?
Does the existence of independent statements like the continuum hypothesis count against Platonism or for it?
Could an alien civilisation have a completely different mathematics, or would they inevitably discover the same primes?
